compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
Both colleagues have the same information, deadlines, responsibilities and authorisations. They follow the same site procedures.

The fictional rows compare ways to manage an authorised commitment or illustrate evidence and criteria both types can use. Either person can take either approach.

| Same situation | One approach | Another approach | Preference illustrated |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The same open work order needs a follow-up time | Agree on a provisional slot and when to review it | Keep two authorised slots available until the same checks are complete | J/P: settling a commitment versus keeping alternatives open |
| The same handover entry needs a named owner | Confirm one available owner for the next step | Record the person responsible for confirming which of two authorised colleagues will take the next step | J/P: settling the assignment versus preserving options within the reporting rules |
| A progress update is due while the same evidence is pending | Confirm a provisional review time and report the current uncertainty | Keep two review times available and report when one will be chosen | J/P: setting a provisional plan versus holding alternatives. Neither approach reports an unverified conclusion |
| Both record the same verified deviation and follow the site procedure | Agree on an authorised date for the next review | Keep two authorised review dates open until availability is confirmed | J/P: handling a scheduling commitment. Acceptance criteria stay the same |
| The team reviews the same shift records | Check the recorded outcome against the acceptance criterion | Check concrete observations against earlier records under comparable conditions | Shared S and T: evidence and consistent reasoning are useful to either person |

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Two colleagues may ask for the same records and measurements at shift change. They can still differ on which follow-up commitments to settle immediately.

Work requirements, training and access to information can explain those choices. Quietness, punctuality and the amount someone writes cannot establish either type.

I addresses the orientation of attention and energy. S addresses the information someone tends to trust. T addresses decision criteria. The letters say little about whether someone speaks up in one particular meeting.

The J/P distinction can be illustrated by how the team handles an authorised plan: agreeing on a provisional commitment now or keeping feasible options open until new information arrives. Either type can use both approaches.

### ISTJ and ISTP: what to agree at handover and what to leave open

In a fictional handover, two qualified colleagues have the same records, responsibilities and deadline. Both document the known facts and uncertainty. One option is to settle a provisional follow-up slot and set a review point. Another is to keep two authorised slots open until the outstanding information arrives.

A provisional slot gives the next shift a commitment it can plan around, though the team may need to revise it. Keeping options open preserves flexibility, but the next shift needs to know who will choose and when.

Either person can make a firm arrangement or keep options open. Required signatures, reporting and any safety action still follow the site procedure.
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
These three fictional scenarios concern communication and follow-up. Authorised personnel decide about stops, isolation, inspection and release under site procedures.

Clarify who owns the handover record and who is authorised to make a technical decision. Either type can take either role if qualified.

### ISTJ and ISTP: handing over three open work orders at shift change

(Fictional example) The night shift passes on three open work orders: unusual pump vibration, a conveyor tracking issue and a recorded drop in oil level. The day shift has the same log and a morning meeting. The site’s procedures and authorised personnel govern any equipment decision.

Both colleagues document the same observations and assign responsibility for following up. One option is to assign a provisional time for each review. Another is to keep authorised review slots open until outstanding information arrives. Either type can use both approaches.

The next shift needs to know what is confirmed, what remains uncertain and who will provide the next update. No follow-up arrangement changes what is required for any inspection or release.

In the site’s approved handover format, distinguish closed items with evidence from open items with an owner, a next step and a deadline. If the open list is blank, check it against the work-order system before assuming nothing remains.

### ISTJ and ISTP: a delivery of bearings that does not match the specification

(Fictional example) A supplier delivers a batch of bearings that differs from the purchase order. Both colleagues have the same report and replacement estimate. Authorised staff review the discrepancy under the site’s quality process.

With the same verified facts, one colleague could agree a provisional review date, while another could hold two review dates open until the supplier replies. Either type can do either. The review date does not determine whether the parts are compliant.

The decision about acceptance or alternative use depends on the technical requirements, verified records and approval by authorised staff. Both types follow the same requirements.

### ISTJ and ISTP: the roof at home leaks, and how the brothers split the cost

(Fictional example) After heavy rain, two siblings receive the same report of a leak at their parents’ home. They share the same budget and seek a qualified roofer’s assessment. Neither inspects the roof themselves.

Either sibling could agree a provisional appointment with a contractor and say when they will confirm it. Either could keep two available appointments open until they hear back from the roofer. The choice concerns logistics, and the roofer establishes the cause and scope of any repair.

Either sibling might ask for written warranty terms or compare payment schedules. Before agreeing to share the cost, identify the required work, what the quote covers and when any provisional arrangement will be confirmed.

compare_blocks.body:
Judging and Perceiving describe the outward-facing process in the model. Either type can plan ahead or revise a schedule when facts change.

Tidiness, speech and the length of a record cannot identify type. The team’s reporting requirements determine what belongs in the handover.

Following a procedure and interpreting observations are skills either type can develop. Training, responsibilities and authorisation shape what each person can do.

Both types follow the site’s procedures for stops, isolation, inspection and release. A willingness to bypass a procedure is unrelated to the J/P comparison.

body: **Framework sources**: the definitions of the preferences follow the [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.themyersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts); the type-dynamics framework follows the [Foundation's note on type dynamics](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/).

**Function-stack convention**: this page uses Fi for ISTJ’s tertiary Feeling and Ni for ISTP’s tertiary Intuition. The Foundation’s overview allows either orientation for each. These positions describe the model and cannot predict behaviour, competence or compatibility.
**Editorial fiction**: the handover, delivery and roof scenarios and the comparison table illustrate fictional decisions. They provide no frequency data or operating instructions.

**Scope limits**: this page offers no statistical sample or effect data; the cited sources support the framework and the preference definitions only. Results are not for ranking ability, hiring screens or predicting relationships; decisions about stops, isolation, inspection, release and alternative use belong with authorised personnel under the procedure and the technical documents. The FermatMind assessment uses a separate item bank and scoring; its scope is set out in the [scoring and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).

compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
Both colleagues have the same information, deadlines, responsibilities and authorisations. They follow the same site procedures.

The fictional rows compare ways to manage an authorised commitment or illustrate evidence and criteria both types can use. Either person can take either approach.

| Same situation | One approach | Another approach | Preference illustrated |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The same open work order needs a follow-up time | Agree on a provisional slot and when to review it | Keep two authorised slots available until the same checks are complete | J/P: settling a commitment versus keeping alternatives open |
| The same handover entry needs a named owner | Confirm one available owner for the next step | Record the person responsible for confirming which of two authorised colleagues will take the next step | J/P: settling the assignment versus preserving options within the reporting rules |
| A progress update is due while the same evidence is pending | Confirm a provisional review time and report the current uncertainty | Keep two review times available and report when one will be chosen | J/P: setting a provisional plan versus holding alternatives. Neither approach reports an unverified conclusion |
| Both record the same verified deviation and follow the site procedure | Agree on an authorised date for the next review | Keep two authorised review dates open until availability is confirmed | J/P: handling a scheduling commitment. Acceptance criteria stay the same |
| The team reviews the same shift records | Check the recorded outcome against the acceptance criterion | Check concrete observations against earlier records under comparable conditions | Shared S and T: evidence and consistent reasoning are useful to either person |
| The same unusual noise has been reported | Record the verified observation in the required report | Add the relevant confirmed service history to the same report | Shared S: both use concrete evidence. The site determines the response |
compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Two colleagues may ask for the same records and measurements at shift change. They can still differ on which follow-up commitments to settle immediately.

Work requirements, training and access to information can explain those choices. Quietness, punctuality and the amount someone writes cannot establish either type.

I addresses the orientation of attention and energy. S addresses the information someone tends to trust. T addresses decision criteria. The letters say little about whether someone speaks up in one particular meeting.

The J/P distinction can be illustrated by how the team handles an authorised plan: agreeing on a provisional commitment now or keeping feasible options open until new information arrives. Either type can use both approaches.

### ISTJ and ISTP: what to agree at handover and what to leave open

In a fictional handover, two qualified colleagues have the same records, responsibilities and deadline. Both document the known facts and uncertainty. One option is to settle a provisional follow-up slot and set a review point. Another is to keep two authorised slots open until the outstanding information arrives.

A provisional slot gives the next shift a commitment it can plan around, though the team may need to revise it. Keeping options open preserves flexibility, but the next shift needs to know who will choose and when.

Either person can make a firm arrangement or keep options open. Required signatures, reporting and any safety action still follow the site procedure.
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
These three fictional scenarios concern communication and follow-up. Authorised personnel decide about stops, isolation, inspection and release under site procedures.

Clarify who owns the handover record and who is authorised to make a technical decision. Either type can take either role if qualified.

### ISTJ and ISTP: handing over three open work orders at shift change

(Fictional example) The night shift passes on three open work orders: unusual pump vibration, a conveyor tracking issue and a recorded drop in oil level. The day shift has the same log and a morning meeting. The site’s procedures and authorised personnel govern any equipment decision.

Both colleagues document the same observations and assign responsibility for following up. One option is to assign a provisional time for each review. Another is to keep authorised review slots open until outstanding information arrives. Either type can use both approaches.

The next shift needs to know what is confirmed, what remains uncertain and who will provide the next update. No follow-up arrangement changes what is required for any inspection or release.

In the site’s approved handover format, distinguish closed items with evidence from open items with an owner, a next step and a deadline. If the open list is blank, check it against the work-order system before assuming nothing remains.

### ISTJ and ISTP: a delivery of bearings that does not match the specification

(Fictional example) A supplier delivers a batch of bearings that differs from the purchase order. Both colleagues have the same report and replacement estimate. Authorised staff review the discrepancy under the site’s quality process.

With the same verified facts, one colleague could agree a provisional review date, while another could hold two review dates open until the supplier replies. Either type can do either. The review date does not determine whether the parts are compliant.

The decision about acceptance or alternative use depends on the technical requirements, verified records and approval by authorised staff. Both types follow the same requirements.

### ISTJ and ISTP: the roof at home leaks, and how the brothers split the cost

(Fictional example) After heavy rain, two siblings receive the same report of a leak at their parents’ home. They share the same budget and seek a qualified roofer’s assessment. Neither inspects the roof themselves.

Either sibling could agree a provisional appointment with a contractor and say when they will confirm it. Either could keep two available appointments open until they hear back from the roofer. The choice concerns logistics, and the roofer establishes the cause and scope of any repair.

Either sibling might ask for written warranty terms or compare payment schedules. Before agreeing to share the cost, identify the required work, what the quote covers and when any provisional arrangement will be confirmed.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
Judging and Perceiving describe the outward-facing process in the model. Either type can plan ahead or revise a schedule when facts change.

Tidiness, speech and the length of a record cannot identify type. The team’s reporting requirements determine what belongs in the handover.

Following a procedure and interpreting observations are skills either type can develop. Training, responsibilities and authorisation shape what each person can do.

Both types follow the site’s procedures for stops, isolation, inspection and release. A willingness to bypass a procedure is unrelated to the J/P comparison.

faq_blocks.answer:
A single handover cannot distinguish ISTJ from ISTP. Roles, deadlines and what the previous shift recorded affect what each person does.

For reflection, compare situations where you had the same freedom to settle a plan or keep options open. That illustrates J/P without turning the sequence of actions into a typing rule.
faq_blocks.question: Looking only at the handover moment, how can they be told apart?

faq_blocks.answer:
Both are introverted types, so the outward-facing process is auxiliary. ISTJ’s J identifies judging (Te), and ISTP’s P identifies perceiving (Se). Their dominant processes therefore differ too.

In the convention used here, ISTJ is Si–Te–Fi–Ne and ISTP is Ti–Se–Ni–Fe. Match the families by name: Si with Se, Te with Ti, Fi with Fe and Ne with Ni. Their orientations differ in these two full stacks. The Foundation’s overview also allows Fe or Fi for ISTJ’s tertiary Feeling and Ne or Ni for ISTP’s tertiary Intuition.
faq_blocks.question: One letter apart — why do all four function names change?

faq_blocks.answer:
Yes. Either type can write a detailed record or revise a plan. Required signatures, urgent actions and reporting follow the same procedure.

The useful question is what the next shift needs to know and which commitments the team is authorised to make. Record uncertainty alongside confirmed information.
faq_blocks.question: Can an ISTP write a detailed handover and an ISTJ change a plan quickly?

faq_blocks.answer:
Either type can develop maintenance and dispatch skills. The relevant factors are training, practical experience and authorisation.

Try a fictional handover exercise. Identify what is verified, what remains open and which items need escalation. Compare the result with the role’s handover requirements to see where more practice would help.
faq_blocks.question: Which of the two is better suited to equipment maintenance or shift dispatch?

faq_blocks.answer:
The next shift can miss an unresolved item if the handover leaves out who owns it, what is uncertain or when to expect an update.

Use the approved format to record open items, their owners and deadlines. Follow the site’s procedures for safety or stoppages. Apply those requirements whether the team settles a provisional time or keeps authorised alternatives open.
faq_blocks.question: Working the same shift, where does the handover most often jam?

faq_blocks.answer:
Real decisions can help you reflect. A few choices made under particular work requirements cannot establish a stable type.

Compare the questionnaire, version, language and scoring notes. If the tool reports J/P separately, check how it explains that result. Review choices you could actually make, and consider how work requirements shaped your answers.

body: **Framework sources**: the definitions of the preferences follow the [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.themyersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts); the type-dynamics framework follows the [Foundation's note on type dynamics](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/).

**Function-stack convention**: this page uses Fi for ISTJ’s tertiary Feeling and Ni for ISTP’s tertiary Intuition. The Foundation’s overview allows either orientation for each. These positions describe the model and cannot predict behaviour, competence or compatibility.
**Editorial fiction**: the handover, delivery and roof scenarios and the comparison table illustrate fictional decisions. They provide no frequency data or operating instructions.

**Scope limits**: this page offers no statistical sample or effect data; the cited sources support the framework and the preference definitions only. Results are not for ranking ability, hiring screens or predicting relationships; decisions about stops, isolation, inspection, release and alternative use belong with authorised personnel under the procedure and the technical documents. The FermatMind assessment uses a separate item bank and scoring; its scope is set out in the [scoring and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).

This page uses the stacks ISTJ Si–Te–Fi–Ne and ISTP Ti–Se–Ni–Fe. Both include Sensing, Thinking, Feeling and Intuition, but all four labels differ under this convention. Sources vary in how they label the tertiary orientation.

The stacks describe the model. A single shift handover cannot establish type, workplace competence or fit for a job.

sections.body_md:
ISTJ and ISTP share Introversion (I), Sensing (S) and Thinking (T). Their only letter difference is Judging (J) versus Perceiving (P).

- **Introversion (I):** attention and energy tend to turn inward, toward ideas, memory and reflection.
- **Sensing (S):** concrete observations and experience carry more weight when taking in information.
- **Thinking (T):** decisions tend to emphasise logically consistent criteria.
- **Judging versus Perceiving (J/P):** in type dynamics, J points to an outward judging process and P to an outward perceiving process. Either type can settle a plan or keep options open.

For introverted types, the dominant process faces inward and the auxiliary faces outward. ISTJ uses extraverted Thinking (Te) as its auxiliary, paired with dominant introverted Sensing (Si). ISTP uses extraverted Sensing (Se), paired with dominant introverted Thinking (Ti).

This page uses the stacks ISTJ Si–Te–Fi–Ne and ISTP Ti–Se–Ni–Fe. Both include Sensing, Thinking, Feeling and Intuition, but all four labels differ under this convention. Sources vary in how they label the tertiary orientation.

The stacks describe the model. A single shift handover cannot establish type, workplace competence or fit for a job.
sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Two colleagues may ask for the same records and measurements at shift change. They can still differ on which follow-up commitments to settle immediately.

Work requirements, training and access to information can explain those choices. Quietness, punctuality and the amount someone writes cannot establish either type.

I addresses the orientation of attention and energy. S addresses the information someone tends to trust. T addresses decision criteria. The letters say little about whether someone speaks up in one particular meeting.

The J/P distinction can be illustrated by how the team handles an authorised plan: agreeing on a provisional commitment now or keeping feasible options open until new information arrives. Either type can use both approaches.

### ISTJ and ISTP: what to agree at handover and what to leave open

In a fictional handover, two qualified colleagues have the same records, responsibilities and deadline. Both document the known facts and uncertainty. One option is to settle a provisional follow-up slot and set a review point. Another is to keep two authorised slots open until the outstanding information arrives.

A provisional slot gives the next shift a commitment it can plan around, though the team may need to revise it. Keeping options open preserves flexibility, but the next shift needs to know who will choose and when.

Either person can make a firm arrangement or keep options open. Required signatures, reporting and any safety action still follow the site procedure.
sections.title: ISTJ and ISTP: what they share, and where J/P splits

sections.body_md:
Both colleagues have the same information, deadlines, responsibilities and authorisations. They follow the same site procedures.

The fictional rows compare ways to manage an authorised commitment or illustrate evidence and criteria both types can use. Either person can take either approach.

| Same situation | One approach | Another approach | Preference illustrated |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The same open work order needs a follow-up time | Agree on a provisional slot and when to review it | Keep two authorised slots available until the same checks are complete | J/P: settling a commitment versus keeping alternatives open |
| The same handover entry needs a named owner | Confirm one available owner for the next step | Record the person responsible for confirming which of two authorised colleagues will take the next step | J/P: settling the assignment versus preserving options within the reporting rules |
| A progress update is due while the same evidence is pending | Confirm a provisional review time and report the current uncertainty | Keep two review times available and report when one will be chosen | J/P: setting a provisional plan versus holding alternatives. Neither approach reports an unverified conclusion |
| Both record the same verified deviation and follow the site procedure | Agree on an authorised date for the next review | Keep two authorised review dates open until availability is confirmed | J/P: handling a scheduling commitment. Acceptance criteria stay the same |
| The team reviews the same shift records | Check the recorded outcome against the acceptance criterion | Check concrete observations against earlier records under comparable conditions | Shared S and T: evidence and consistent reasoning are useful to either person |
| The same unusual noise has been reported | Record the verified observation in the required report | Add the relevant confirmed service history to the same report | Shared S: both use concrete evidence. The site determines the response |
sections.title: ISTJ and ISTP in one minute

sections.body_md:
These three fictional scenarios concern communication and follow-up. Authorised personnel decide about stops, isolation, inspection and release under site procedures.

Clarify who owns the handover record and who is authorised to make a technical decision. Either type can take either role if qualified.

### ISTJ and ISTP: handing over three open work orders at shift change

(Fictional example) The night shift passes on three open work orders: unusual pump vibration, a conveyor tracking issue and a recorded drop in oil level. The day shift has the same log and a morning meeting. The site’s procedures and authorised personnel govern any equipment decision.

Both colleagues document the same observations and assign responsibility for following up. One option is to assign a provisional time for each review. Another is to keep authorised review slots open until outstanding information arrives. Either type can use both approaches.

The next shift needs to know what is confirmed, what remains uncertain and who will provide the next update. No follow-up arrangement changes what is required for any inspection or release.

In the site’s approved handover format, distinguish closed items with evidence from open items with an owner, a next step and a deadline. If the open list is blank, check it against the work-order system before assuming nothing remains.

### ISTJ and ISTP: a delivery of bearings that does not match the specification

(Fictional example) A supplier delivers a batch of bearings that differs from the purchase order. Both colleagues have the same report and replacement estimate. Authorised staff review the discrepancy under the site’s quality process.

With the same verified facts, one colleague could agree a provisional review date, while another could hold two review dates open until the supplier replies. Either type can do either. The review date does not determine whether the parts are compliant.

The decision about acceptance or alternative use depends on the technical requirements, verified records and approval by authorised staff. Both types follow the same requirements.

### ISTJ and ISTP: the roof at home leaks, and how the brothers split the cost

(Fictional example) After heavy rain, two siblings receive the same report of a leak at their parents’ home. They share the same budget and seek a qualified roofer’s assessment. Neither inspects the roof themselves.

Either sibling could agree a provisional appointment with a contractor and say when they will confirm it. Either could keep two available appointments open until they hear back from the roofer. The choice concerns logistics, and the roofer establishes the cause and scope of any repair.

Either sibling might ask for written warranty terms or compare payment schedules. Before agreeing to share the cost, identify the required work, what the quote covers and when any provisional arrangement will be confirmed.
sections.title: ISTJ and ISTP in three fictional scenarios

sections.body_md:
Judging and Perceiving describe the outward-facing process in the model. Either type can plan ahead or revise a schedule when facts change.

Tidiness, speech and the length of a record cannot identify type. The team’s reporting requirements determine what belongs in the handover.

Following a procedure and interpreting observations are skills either type can develop. Training, responsibilities and authorisation shape what each person can do.

Both types follow the site’s procedures for stops, isolation, inspection and release. A willingness to bypass a procedure is unrelated to the J/P comparison.
sections.title: ISTJ and ISTP: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
If results alternate between ISTJ and ISTP, compare the assessment, version, language and scoring notes. Think about whether you answered from your own preferences or from what the job required.

Recall several comparable decisions where you had room to choose. Record what you wanted to settle, what you wanted to leave open and what information could change your mind. Keep required steps separate from choices. Use the notes for reflection without scoring them.
sections.title: ISTJ and ISTP: how to keep observing

items.answer:
A single handover cannot distinguish ISTJ from ISTP. Roles, deadlines and what the previous shift recorded affect what each person does.

For reflection, compare situations where you had the same freedom to settle a plan or keep options open. That illustrates J/P without turning the sequence of actions into a typing rule.
items.question: Looking only at the handover moment, how can they be told apart?

items.answer:
Both are introverted types, so the outward-facing process is auxiliary. ISTJ’s J identifies judging (Te), and ISTP’s P identifies perceiving (Se). Their dominant processes therefore differ too.

In the convention used here, ISTJ is Si–Te–Fi–Ne and ISTP is Ti–Se–Ni–Fe. Match the families by name: Si with Se, Te with Ti, Fi with Fe and Ne with Ni. Their orientations differ in these two full stacks. The Foundation’s overview also allows Fe or Fi for ISTJ’s tertiary Feeling and Ne or Ni for ISTP’s tertiary Intuition.
items.question: One letter apart — why do all four function names change?

items.answer:
Yes. Either type can write a detailed record or revise a plan. Required signatures, urgent actions and reporting follow the same procedure.

The useful question is what the next shift needs to know and which commitments the team is authorised to make. Record uncertainty alongside confirmed information.
items.question: Can an ISTP write a detailed handover and an ISTJ change a plan quickly?

items.answer:
Either type can develop maintenance and dispatch skills. The relevant factors are training, practical experience and authorisation.

Try a fictional handover exercise. Identify what is verified, what remains open and which items need escalation. Compare the result with the role’s handover requirements to see where more practice would help.
items.question: Which of the two is better suited to equipment maintenance or shift dispatch?

items.answer:
The next shift can miss an unresolved item if the handover leaves out who owns it, what is uncertain or when to expect an update.

Use the approved format to record open items, their owners and deadlines. Follow the site’s procedures for safety or stoppages. Apply those requirements whether the team settles a provisional time or keeps authorised alternatives open.
items.question: Working the same shift, where does the handover most often jam?

items.answer:
Real decisions can help you reflect. A few choices made under particular work requirements cannot establish a stable type.

Compare the questionnaire, version, language and scoring notes. If the tool reports J/P separately, check how it explains that result. Review choices you could actually make, and consider how work requirements shaped your answers.

sections.body_md:
**Framework sources**: the definitions of the preferences follow the [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.themyersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts); the type-dynamics framework follows the [Foundation's note on type dynamics](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/).

**Function-stack convention**: this page uses Fi for ISTJ’s tertiary Feeling and Ni for ISTP’s tertiary Intuition. The Foundation’s overview allows either orientation for each. These positions describe the model and cannot predict behaviour, competence or compatibility.

**Editorial fiction**: the handover, delivery and roof scenarios and the comparison table illustrate fictional decisions. They provide no frequency data or operating instructions.

**Scope limits**: this page offers no statistical sample or effect data; the cited sources support the framework and the preference definitions only. Results are not for ranking ability, hiring screens or predicting relationships; decisions about stops, isolation, inspection, release and alternative use belong with authorised personnel under the procedure and the technical documents. The FermatMind assessment uses a separate item bank and scoring; its scope is set out in the [scoring and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).
